planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm, or start indoors 3-4 weeks early for an earlier bloom flush. Goldfinger is a compact selection of Mexican sunflower bred to stay under 3 feet, roughly half the height of taller types like Torch, making it useful where a shorter, self-supporting plant is needed.

directions: Sow in full sun in lean, well-drained soil, since rich soil produces excess foliage at the expense of flowers. Goldfinger keeps the same intense orange-red daisy blooms and heat tolerance as taller Mexican sunflower cultivars but on a shorter, sturdier, more compact plant that rarely needs staking, making it a better fit for smaller beds, containers, and the front-to-mid border. It flowers continuously from midsummer through frost and is a strong draw for monarchs, swallowtails, and other nectar-seeking pollinators. Deadhead spent blooms to keep the compact plants tidy and encourage continued flowering.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring 2-4 weeks before the last frost, or in late summer in mild-winter areas for an overwintered crop; Graceland resents transplanting and should be sown where it is to flower.

directions: Sow seed directly and press it onto the soil surface, since light aids germination and the taproot resents disturbance; thin seedlings to 9-12 inches apart. Graceland was selected specifically for the cut-flower trade, producing notably larger, more rounded lace-like white umbels on taller, sturdier stems than the wild species, which is why it has become a favorite of florists and flower farmers alike. The strong stems hold up well in transport and arranging, with a vase life commonly reaching a week or more. Give plants full sun and even moisture, and stake or grow through support netting in windy sites since the tall stems can lean under the weight of the large flower heads.

planting.note: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked in late winter or early spring, or in fall in mild-winter areas for earlier spring bloom; nigella resents transplanting and is best sown where it is to flower.

directions: Direct sow a quarter-inch deep in well-drained soil in full sun; the fine taproot rarely survives transplanting. Cramer's Plum opens pure white, many-petaled flowers ringed in the same lacy green foliage typical of love-in-a-mist, but its real distinction comes after bloom, when the flowers give way to large, inflated, balloon-like seed pods that ripen to a rich, deep plum-purple, far more saturated than the pale, streaky pods of older strains. Grow it as much for the pods as the flowers — they hold their color and form beautifully when cut fresh or air-dried for arrangements. Like other nigella, it grows and blooms fastest in cool weather and will self-seed readily where happy.

common_name: Sparkler White Cleome (Compact Spineless Spider Flower)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, pressing seed onto the surface since light aids germination; transplant after frost danger has passed, or direct sow once soil is warm.

directions: Sparkler White carries the same compact, spineless habit as the rest of the Sparkler breeding line, making it far easier to handle around beds and pathways than old-fashioned heirloom cleome. Its large, airy, spidery flower clusters open in clean white with long, whiskery pink-tinged stamens, giving a fresh, luminous look to summer borders and cut arrangements. Plants branch naturally and stay shorter and tidier than heirloom Queen-series types, so they rarely need staking. Removing developing seed pods regularly keeps plants flowering continuously into fall rather than shifting energy into seed production.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Cut Flowers

common_name: Sparkler Rose Cleome (Compact Spineless Spider Flower)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, pressing seed onto the surface since light aids germination; transplant after frost danger has passed, or direct sow once soil is warm.

directions: Sparkler Rose shares the compact, spineless plants and heavy, non-stop flowering of the Sparkler breeding line, but carries rich rose-pink flowers in large, rounded, spidery clusters atop strong, well-branched stems. Its shorter stature compared to heirloom Queen-series cleome makes it well suited to large containers and mixed borders where taller old-fashioned types would need staking. Plants keep blooming through summer heat and humidity, drawing hummingbirds and butterflies, and the flower clusters hold well when cut for arrangements. Regularly removing developing seed pods encourages continued bloom rather than a shift to seed set.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, pressing seed onto the soil surface without covering since light aids germination; transplant after frost danger has passed into a spot where the unusual bicolor blooms can be viewed up close.

directions: Tinkerbell produces slender, pale green tubular flowers that flare open to reveal a rosy, deep maroon-red face centered on bright blue stamens, an unusual bicolor combination that sets it apart from the plain white or solid-color flowering tobaccos more commonly grown. Like other flowering tobacco, the trumpets release their sweetest fragrance in the evening and at dusk, drawing sphinx moths along with daytime pollinators. The upright, airy plants work well massed in a border or grown in large containers near a patio or window where the scent and unusual coloring can be appreciated after sundown. Deadhead spent flowers to keep the plants tidy and encourage continued bloom through summer into fall.

common_name: Perfume Deep Purple Nicotiana (Evening-Fragrant Compact Flowering Tobacco)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, surface-sowing without covering since seed needs light to germinate; transplant into beds or containers after frost danger has passed.

directions: Perfume Deep Purple is an All-America Selections award-winning nicotiana bred for a compact, uniform habit and unusually strong evening fragrance in a garden-scaled plant. Star-shaped, deep purple flowers cover the bushy mounds from early summer to frost, releasing an intoxicating, clove-like scent that intensifies after dusk, making it well suited to plantings near patios, decks, and windows where the perfume can be enjoyed at night. Its shorter, more compact stature compared to species-type nicotiana means it needs no staking and performs well in containers as well as garden beds. Deadhead spent flowers periodically to keep plants tidy and blooming heavily through summer heat.
